error_modes.label: INTERRUPTED CHECKLIST NOT RESTARTED AT THE CORRECT POINT

texts.0: SP, due to resuming an interrupted checklist from the point of recall instead of restarting at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, omitted a checklist item and did not positively confirm completion. A new checklist was then started before the previous one had been completed, so the omission was never detected. The aircraft was operated in a configuration not authorized for that phase of flight and the IP had to direct the missing actions.
texts.1: SP, due to picking the checklist back up one step after the interruption rather than two to three steps prior to it, left an item unconfirmed and did not verify completion of the checklist as a whole. The omission was identified and corrected only after a verbal reminder from the IP. The configuration was restored, but the delay left the aircraft at the limit of the acceptable standard for that phase.
texts.2: SP, due to a radio call that interrupted the checklist flow, initially resumed at the wrong point in the sequence. SP recognized the break, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step and positively confirmed completion before starting the next checklist. No item was omitted and no IP prompting was required.
texts.3: SP attempted every checklist without interruption and, when an interruption occurred, restarted at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step. Completion of each checklist was positively confirmed and no new checklist was started before the previous one had been completed.
texts.4: SP protected each checklist from interruption by sequencing the other cockpit tasks around it, and whenever an interruption could not be avoided restarted well before the affected step and verified the whole sequence afterwards. Every checklist was positively confirmed complete, in order, with no omissions and without any reference prompt.
texts.marginal: SP completed all checklists and confirmed them, but after each interruption the resumption point was chosen by memory and the back-up steps were taken only after a visible pause for thought. The trend was toward relying on recall of where the flow was broken rather than on the published restart technique. SP is expected to restart at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step as a matter of habit.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the checklist-interruption restart technique, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance, and SP is expected to need less of that guidance on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP restarted an interrupted checklist at the correct point inside the code 1 band, an item left unconfirmed until it was pointed out. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to restart at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step as a matter of habit.
texts_at.2: SP restarted an interrupted checklist at the correct point inside the code 2 band, correcting a resumption initially made at the wrong point in the sequence. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the break in the flow a little sooner so the restart point is chosen correctly the first time.
texts_at.3: SP attempted every checklist without interruption and, when an interruption occurred, restarted at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, with one restart point chosen a little late in the recall. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to choose that point as promptly as the rest.

texts_above.1: SP restarted an interrupted checklist at the correct point, with one item left unconfirmed after the interruption. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a break in the checklist flow, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step and positively confirmed completion before starting the next checklist, with no item omitted. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady checklist restart discipline.
texts_above.3: SP attempted every checklist without interruption and, when an interruption occurred, restarted at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, positively confirming completion of each checklist before starting the next. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate checklist restart discipline.
texts_above.4: SP protected each checklist from interruption by sequencing other cockpit tasks around it, and whenever an interruption could not be avoided restarted well before the affected step and verified the whole sequence afterward. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary checklist restart discipline.

error_modes.label: OPERATIONS CHECK INTERVAL AND FENCE IN/OUT DISCIPLINE

texts.0: SP, due to concentrating exclusively on the maneuver sequence during area work, did not perform the operations check at any point and entered and left the MOA without a FENCE check. Fuel quantity and balance, engine indications, NAVAIDS and equipment were therefore never verified during the working period. The IP had to direct the checks and the aircraft state was found outside the briefed fuel and configuration expectations.
texts.1: SP, due to a loss of time awareness while maneuvering, allowed the interval between operations checks to stretch well beyond the approximate fifteen minute interval the Techniques and Procedures Manual gives and omitted the FENCE-out check on leaving the MOA. The checks were accomplished only after the IP called for them on each occasion. The engine and fuel state were confirmed acceptable but only at the limit of the briefed margins.
texts.2: SP, due to sequencing several maneuvers without reference to the clock, let the operations check slip past the fifteen minute point. SP noticed the omission without prompting, completed the full check and thereafter used the quarter hour as the trigger for the following checks. The remaining checks were on time and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP performed the operations check approximately every fifteen minutes while accomplishing area work and completed a FENCE check on entering and again on leaving the MOA. Fuel, engine, NAVAIDS, communications and equipment were verified at each check and the checks were not repeated between maneuvers flown in a series.
texts.4: SP anchored the operations checks to the quarter hour and used the clock stopwatch so that no check was late, and the FENCE-in and FENCE-out checks were completed precisely at the MOA boundaries. Each check was accomplished without interrupting the flow of the profile and every deviation in fuel or engine indications would have been caught at its earliest point.
texts.marginal: SP accomplished the operations checks and both FENCE checks within the required standard, but the timing depended on remembering to look at the clock and one interval ran close to the fifteen minute limit before the check was started. The trend was toward checks triggered by a gap in the profile rather than by time. SP is expected to tie the operations check to the stopwatch or to the quarter hour so the interval is protected.

texts_at.0: SP practiced operations-check and FENCE timing, with the IP prompting each action verbally as the item developed, this being SP's first presentation of the item. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point, and SP is expected to take over more of the sequence without prompting next time.
texts_at.1: SP performed the operations check and the FENCE checks on their intervals inside the code 1 band, the interval stretching well past the standard before the checks were accomplished on prompting. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to tie the operations check to the stopwatch or to the quarter hour so the interval is protected.
texts_at.2: SP performed the operations check and the FENCE checks on their intervals inside the code 2 band, correcting an interval that had slipped past the fifteen minute point before it was noticed unaided. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to reference the clock a little more often so the interval does not need catching up.
texts_at.3: SP performed the operations check approximately every fifteen minutes while accomplishing area work and completed a FENCE check on entering and again on leaving the MOA, with one check triggered by a gap in the profile rather than by time. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to trigger that check by time as well.

texts_above.1: SP performed the operations check and the FENCE checks on their intervals, with one interval stretching well past the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP noticed the operations check slipping past the fifteen minute point without prompting, completed the full check and used the quarter hour as the trigger for the checks that followed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable operations check and FENCE timing.
texts_above.3: SP performed the operations check approximately every fifteen minutes while accomplishing area work and completed a FENCE check on entering and again on leaving the MOA, verifying fuel, engine, NAVAIDS, communications and equipment at each one. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good operations check and FENCE timing.
texts_above.4: SP anchored the operations checks to the quarter hour and the stopwatch so no check was late, completing the FENCE-in and FENCE-out checks precisely at the MOA boundaries without interrupting the flow of the profile. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior operations check and FENCE timing.

error_modes.label: CLEF CHECK PRIOR TO STALLS, SPINS AND AEROBATICS

texts.0: SP, due to proceeding directly from the previous maneuver into the setup, did not accomplish the CLEF check before the stall and spin series. The area and the CWS panel were not cleared, loose items were left unstowed and the fuel balance was not verified against the fifty pound limit. The IP had to stop the setup, direct the check and reposition the aircraft before the maneuver could be attempted.
texts.1: SP, due to treating the CLEF items as covered by the earlier FENCE check, entered the aerobatic setup with the fuel balance unverified and the clearing turn incomplete. The check was accomplished item by item only after the IP called for it, and the fuel balance was compared with the fifty pound limit only at that point. The maneuver was flown to standard but only after the delay imposed by the late check.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed transition from the previous maneuver, began the entry setup before completing the CLEF items. SP recognized the omission without prompting, stopped the setup, cleared the area and the CWS panel, confirmed loose items stowed, engine within limits and fuel balance well inside the fifty pound limit before proceeding. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP accomplished the CLEF check before each stall, spin and aerobatic maneuver, clearing the area and the CWS panel, confirming loose items stowed, engine indications within limits and fuel balance within fifty pounds. The check was not repeated between maneuvers flown in a series, in accordance with the manual.
texts.4: SP completed the CLEF check smoothly ahead of every stalling, spinning and aerobatic sequence, keeping the fuel balance managed so that the imbalance stayed close to zero and clearing the area in a pattern that covered the full maneuvering airspace. The checks were integrated into the setup without any loss of position, energy or time.
texts.marginal: SP completed the CLEF check before each maneuver and the fuel imbalance stayed inside the fifty pound limit, but the items were recited quickly and the clearing turn was abbreviated when the maneuver had to be started before leaving the area. The trend was toward compressing the check under time pressure. SP is expected to keep the clearing and fuel balance items deliberate regardless of the time available.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the CLEF check before the maneuver series, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.
texts_at.1: SP accomplished the CLEF check before the stall, spin and aerobatic series inside the code 1 band, the check completed item by item only after it was called for. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep the clearing and fuel balance items deliberate regardless of the time available.
texts_at.2: SP accomplished the CLEF check before the stall, spin and aerobatic series inside the code 2 band, correcting an entry setup begun before the check was complete. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the omission a little sooner so the setup is stopped before it advances further.
texts_at.3: SP accomplished the CLEF check before each stall, spin and aerobatic maneuver, clearing the area and the CWS panel and confirming loose items, engine and fuel balance, with the clearing turn abbreviated once under time pressure. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to keep that turn to the same standard under pressure.

texts_above.1: SP accomplished the CLEF check before the stall, spin and aerobatic series, with the check completed later than the briefed point. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized an entry setup begun before the CLEF items were complete, stopped the setup and completed the check before proceeding, with no IP intervention required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured CLEF check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP accomplished the CLEF check before each stall, spin and aerobatic maneuver, clearing the area and the CWS panel, confirming loose items stowed, engine indications within limits and fuel balance within the published margin, not repeating the check between maneuvers flown in series. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise CLEF check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP completed the CLEF check smoothly ahead of every stalling, spinning and aerobatic sequence, keeping the fuel imbalance close to zero and clearing the area in a pattern that covered the full maneuvering airspace. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate CLEF check discipline.

error_modes.label: JOKER AND BINGO FUEL AS DECISION GATES

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the regular fuel checks during the sortie, did not use the briefed joker fuel as the transition point and continued the profile past bingo fuel without initiating a recovery. The remaining sortie was flown with no assessment of the fuel required to reach the intended destination. The IP had to direct the recovery, and the aircraft returned with the reserve reduced below the planned figure.
texts.1: SP, due to infrequent fuel checks, passed the pre-planned joker fuel without transitioning to the next phase of the profile and recognized the bingo state only when the IP stated it. The recovery was initiated on IP direction and the aircraft arrived at the destination with the fuel at the minimum required figure. Continuous IP monitoring of the fuel state was necessary.
texts.2: SP, due to concentrating on the maneuver sequence, allowed one fuel check to be missed and passed the joker fuel point unnoticed. SP detected the fuel state at the next check without prompting, terminated the current phase and initiated the recovery well before bingo fuel. The intended destination was reached with the planned reserve intact.
texts.3: SP performed regular fuel checks throughout the mission, used the briefed joker fuel as the trigger for the planned transition and initiated the recovery prior to reaching bingo fuel. The remaining profile was matched to the fuel available and the aircraft arrived at the intended destination with the required fuel.
texts.4: SP integrated the fuel check into every operations check, tracked the trend against the briefed joker and bingo figures and adjusted the sequence of the remaining maneuvers so that each objective was completed before its fuel gate. The recovery was initiated ahead of the plan and the aircraft landed with a comfortable margin above the required fuel.
texts.marginal: SP performed the fuel checks and respected the joker and bingo figures, but the checks were spaced unevenly and the transition at joker fuel followed the figure rather than anticipating it. The trend was toward reading the fuel state as a limit reached rather than as a planning tool. SP is expected to check fuel at regular intervals and to shape the remaining profile before the joker figure is reached.

texts_at.0: SP practiced using joker and bingo fuel as gates, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP used the briefed joker and bingo fuel figures as decision gates inside the code 1 band, the bingo state recognized only after it was stated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to check fuel at regular intervals and shape the remaining profile before the joker figure is reached.
texts_at.2: SP used the briefed joker and bingo fuel figures as decision gates inside the code 2 band, correcting a missed fuel check that had let the joker point pass unnoticed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to space the fuel checks a little more evenly so none is missed.
texts_at.3: SP performed regular fuel checks throughout the mission, used the briefed joker fuel as the trigger for the planned transition and initiated the recovery prior to reaching bingo fuel, with one check spaced a little wider than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to space that check as evenly as the others.

texts_above.1: SP used the briefed joker and bingo fuel figures as decision gates, with the bingo state recognized later than the gate itself. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP detected the fuel state at the next check without prompting after one earlier check was missed, terminating the current phase and initiating the recovery well before bingo fuel. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound use of joker and bingo fuel gates.
texts_above.3: SP performed regular fuel checks throughout the mission, used the briefed joker fuel as the trigger for the planned transition and initiated the recovery prior to reaching bingo fuel, matching the remaining profile to the fuel available. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed use of joker and bingo fuel gates.
texts_above.4: SP integrated the fuel check into every operations check, tracked the trend against the briefed joker and bingo figures and adjusted the sequence of the remaining maneuvers so each objective was completed before its fuel gate. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional use of joker and bingo fuel gates.

error_modes.label: GO-AROUND WHEN THE LANDING ATTEMPT LOOKS OR FEELS WRONG

texts.0: SP, due to an attempt to salvage a landing that was recognized as abnormal, continued the approach with the aircraft out of position and the pattern situation deteriorating instead of executing a go-around. The abnormal situation was not identified as one requiring an immediate go-around and no decision was stated. The IP had to take control and initiate the go-around from an unsafe position.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation to abandon a landing attempt that both looked and felt wrong, continued the approach and initiated the go-around only after the IP directed it. The recovery from the abnormal situation was correct once started, but the delay left the aircraft at the limit of the acceptable standard for the pattern.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial attempt to correct an approach that was developing abnormally, continued briefly before reassessing. SP recognized without prompting that the attempt could not be salvaged, stated the decision and executed a clean go-around from a safe position. Pattern spacing and the traffic situation were preserved and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the traffic pattern promptly and executed a go-around without hesitation when the landing attempt looked or felt wrong. When the location of other traffic was in doubt the tower controller was queried, and the pattern was rejoined in accordance with the published procedure.
texts.4: SP identified the developing abnormality early, stated the go-around decision before the situation degraded and flew the go-around and the re-entry to the pattern precisely, with the tower informed and the traffic picture clarified in advance. No attempt was made to salvage a compromised approach at any point in the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP executed the required go-arounds and kept the pattern within standards, but each decision was taken late in the approach after a period of trying to correct the situation. The trend was toward salvaging first and deciding afterwards. SP is expected to go around immediately when a landing attempt looks or simply feels wrong, without attempting to correct it first.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the go-around judgment on a compromised landing, with the IP providing hands-on guidance on the controls, the sequence still new to SP at this stage of training. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet, and SP is expected to manage more of the sequence unaided on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP recognized an abnormal landing attempt and executed a go-around inside the code 1 band, the go-around initiated only after it was directed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to go around immediately when a landing attempt looks or simply feels wrong, without attempting to correct it first.
texts_at.2: SP recognized an abnormal landing attempt and executed a go-around inside the code 2 band, correcting a brief continuation of the approach before reassessing. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to reassess the approach a little sooner so the continuation is shorter.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the traffic pattern promptly and executed a go-around without hesitation when the landing attempt looked or felt wrong, querying the tower when traffic location was in doubt, with one decision reached a little later in the approach than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to reach that decision as promptly as the others.

texts_above.1: SP recognized an abnormal landing attempt and executed a go-around, with the decision made later than the first indication. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized without prompting that a developing approach could not be salvaged, stated the decision and executed a clean go-around from a safe position with pattern spacing preserved. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good go-around judgment on a compromised landing.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the abnormal situation in the traffic pattern promptly and executed a go-around without hesitation when the landing attempt looked or felt wrong, querying the tower controller when the location of other traffic was in doubt and rejoining the pattern in accordance with the published procedure. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good go-around judgment on a compromised landing.
texts_above.4: SP identified the developing abnormality early, stated the go-around decision before the situation degraded and flew the go-around and re-entry to the pattern precisely, with the tower informed and the traffic picture clarified in advance. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent go-around judgment on a compromised landing.

error_modes.label: STALL INDICATIONS IN THE PATTERN - RECOVERY BEFORE GROUND TRACK

texts.0: SP, due to prioritizing the ground track over the aircraft state, continued to fly the pattern to the runway alignment after stall indications were observed and did not execute the stall recovery procedure. Bank and back stick pressure were maintained while the indications persisted, so the aircraft was flown deeper into the stall regime at low altitude. The IP had to take control, unload the aircraft and complete the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to accept the resulting displacement from the desired ground track, delayed the stall recovery after the indications appeared and applied only a partial unloading. The full recovery procedure was flown only after the IP directed it. The indications ceased and the pattern was continued, but the margin obtained was at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial attempt to hold the turn to final while the indications were developing, was slow to unload the aircraft. SP recognized the priority without prompting, executed the stall recovery procedure and disregarded the ground track until the aircraft was flying cleanly. The pattern was re-established from a safe position and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP recognized the stall indications immediately and executed the stall recovery procedure at once, disregarding the ground track as directed by the manual. Once the aircraft was clean, SP reassessed the position relative to the field and the traffic and either re-entered the pattern or went around as appropriate.
texts.4: SP flew the pattern with an energy margin that kept stall indications from developing, and any indication that did appear was met by an instant recovery, with ground track disregarded and the aircraft unloaded before the condition could progress. The subsequent repositioning was accomplished without any effect on the traffic pattern flow.
texts.marginal: SP recovered correctly whenever stall indications appeared and stayed within the required standards, but the first response each time was a brief glance at the runway alignment before unloading the aircraft. The trend was toward weighing the ground track against the recovery. SP is expected to execute the stall recovery procedure and disregard ground track the moment any stall indication is observed.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the stall-recovery priority in the pattern, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance, and SP is expected to need less of that guidance on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP gave priority to the stall recovery over the ground track inside the code 1 band, the full recovery procedure flown only after it was directed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to execute the stall recovery procedure and disregard ground track the moment any stall indication is observed.
texts_at.2: SP gave priority to the stall recovery over the ground track inside the code 2 band, correcting an initial attempt to hold the turn to final while the indications were developing. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the priority a little sooner so less time passes before the aircraft is unloaded.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the stall indications immediately and executed the stall recovery procedure at once, disregarding the ground track as directed by the manual, with one reassessment of position following a little later than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to reach that reassessment as promptly as the others.

texts_above.1: SP gave priority to the stall recovery over the ground track, with the initial response to the stall indications covering only part of the sequence. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the priority between holding the turn and the stall recovery without prompting, executed the recovery and disregarded the ground track until the aircraft was flying cleanly, with the pattern re-established from a safe position. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent priority given to the stall recovery in the pattern.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the stall indications immediately and executed the stall recovery procedure at once, disregarding the ground track as directed by the manual, and reassessed position relative to the field and the traffic once the aircraft was clean. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined priority given to the stall recovery in the pattern.
texts_above.4: SP flew each pattern with an energy margin that kept stall indications from developing, and held the priority of Techniques and Procedures Manual 5.14 clearly in mind: stall recovery first, ground track disregarded. The turn to final was shaped to the aircraft state rather than to the ground track on every circuit. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless priority given to the stall recovery in the pattern.

error_modes.label: ADVERSE FACTORS - WEATHER, AIRSPACE AND APPROACH RESTRICTIONS, TRAFFIC DENSITY AND AIRCRAFT LIMITATIONS

texts.0: SP, due to mission planning that did not address the forecast weather or the airspace restrictions, went into the sortie without the weather, the area boundaries, the traffic density or the Flight Manual limits in mind. The profile was flown as if none of these factors applied, so no restriction or limit was respected unless the IP raised it. The IP had to take control to keep the aircraft inside the area and within the Flight Manual limits, and the remaining profile was cut short.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete review of the weather and the airspace restrictions in the briefing material, minimized the effect of those factors only in part during the sortie. The area boundaries and the Flight Manual limits were recalled correctly only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. The profile stayed workable, but its margin to the restrictions stayed at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried read of the published restrictions during planning, initially planned the area work without allowing for one of them. SP noticed the gap against the FLIP and the area boundary without prompting, adjusted the profile and kept the working area inside its limits. The effect on the mission was small and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP minimized the effects of adverse factors such as weather conditions, airspace and approach restrictions, high-density traffic, aircraft capabilities and limitations and fuel conservation, and took advantage of the opportunities they left to avoid degrading the mission. The Flight Manual limits and the published restrictions were respected throughout the sortie.
texts.4: SP anticipated every adverse factor in the weather, the airspace, the traffic and the aircraft limits before the briefing ended, and had the profile shaped around them so that the mission lost nothing to any of them. Restrictions and limits were quoted from their source without hesitation.
texts.marginal: SP respected the published restrictions and the Flight Manual limits and kept the mission inside the standard, but the factors were worked into the plan only when the IP raised them in the briefing. The trend was toward reacting to the restrictions rather than planning around them. SP is expected to review the weather, the FLIP restrictions and the aircraft limits before the briefing and to state their effect on the profile.

texts_at.0: SP followed the review of the weather, the airspace restrictions and the Flight Manual limits with the IP naming each factor and its effect on the profile, the habit of working them into the plan being new at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to name the main restriction and the main limit for the sortie before the IP does at the next briefing.
texts_at.1: SP minimized the effect of the weather, the airspace restrictions and the aircraft limits on the profile just inside the standard, one restriction recalled only after the IP prompted it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to review the FLIP restrictions and the Flight Manual limits against the planned profile before the briefing, so none needs a prompt.
texts_at.2: SP minimized the effect of the weather, the airspace restrictions and the aircraft limits on the profile, correcting without prompting a plan that had first left one restriction out. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to read the published restrictions through once more before the briefing, so the plan is complete the first time.
texts_at.3: SP worked the weather, the airspace and approach restrictions, the traffic density and the Flight Manual limits into the profile throughout the sortie, with one factor weighed a little later than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to weigh that factor as promptly as the others.

texts_above.1: SP minimized the effect of the weather, the airspace restrictions and the aircraft limits on the profile, with one restriction recalled after a verbal call from the IP. All the other factors were already in the plan. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP found the omitted restriction in the published material without prompting, adjusted the profile and kept the working area inside its limits. Reading the FLIP restrictions through before the briefing, rather than catching the gap afterward, would remove even that adjustment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent weather and airspace planning.
texts_above.3: SP capitalized on the weather and the airspace available, keeping the profile inside every published restriction and the Flight Manual limits while using the working area to the full. Traffic density and fuel conservation were weighed into each phase of the plan, so the effect of each factor on the mission was minimized rather than absorbed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good anticipation of adverse factors.
texts_above.4: SP identified the factors bearing on the mission before the briefing, matched the profile to the weather, the airspace and approach restrictions, the traffic density and the Flight Manual limits, and kept a better option ready for each. The plan lost no mission value to any of them and needed no change in flight on account of a restriction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior planning around adverse factors.

error_modes.label: RETURN TO BASE OR DEVIATION TO THE ALTERNATE AIRFIELD

texts.0: SP, due to the absence of explicit divert criteria in the mission brief, could not state how the aircraft would return to base from the working area or which alternate airfield would be used. The alternate was not identified, its weather and fuel were not checked, and the return was left to be worked out when it was needed. The IP had to state the return route and the alternate, and direct the return to base.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete study of the return and alternate arrangements, gave a workable return to base but could not state the alternate airfield or the criteria for choosing it. The alternate, its weather and the fuel needed to reach it were supplied only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. The answers were reconstructed rather than recalled and reached the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a planning check that stopped at the home airfield, first named an alternate whose weather had not been looked at. SP noticed the gap without prompting, checked the weather and the fuel needed against the FLIP data and restated a suitable alternate. The return to base stayed safe throughout and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP was able to return to base safely or to deviate to the alternate airfield, stating the route, the alternate, its weather and the fuel needed without prompting. Both were kept current as the sortie progressed.
texts.4: SP kept the return to base and the alternate arrangement continuously current and stated the criteria for choosing between them before they were needed. The alternate's weather and the fuel needed were refreshed at each operations check.
texts.marginal: SP gave a safe return to base and a suitable alternate, but only after thinking them through when asked and without the weather and fuel figures first. The trend was toward building the alternate plan on request. SP is expected to state the return route, the alternate and the criteria for using it as part of the plan.

texts_at.0: SP followed the return and alternate arrangements with the IP naming the alternate, its weather and the fuel needed to reach it, the habit of stating them unprompted being new at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to name the alternate and the criteria for using it before the IP asks on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP was able to return to base safely or to deviate to the alternate at the outer edge of the standard, the alternate and its weather stated only after the IP prompted them. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to brief the alternate, its weather and the fuel needed as part of the plan, from the FLIP data and the squadron SOPs, so none needs prompting.
texts_at.2: SP was able to return to base safely or to deviate to the alternate, correcting without prompting a plan that had named an alternate before its weather was checked. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check the alternate's weather and fuel before naming it, so the first answer is the complete one.
texts_at.3: SP stated the return route, the alternate airfield and the weather and fuel for each throughout the sortie, with the alternate's fuel figure refreshed a little later than the rest. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to refresh that figure as promptly as the others.

texts_above.1: SP stated a safe return to base and an alternate airfield, with the alternate's weather checked after a verbal call from the IP. The rest of the arrangement was already in the plan. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP noticed that the alternate had not yet been checked for weather, checked it against the FLIP data without prompting and restated a suitable alternate with the fuel needed. Checking the weather before naming the alternate would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable return and alternate planning.
texts_above.3: SP kept the return to base and the alternate airfield current throughout the sortie, restating both with the weather and the fuel needed whenever the working area or the fuel state changed. The criteria for choosing between them were stated as part of the plan, not on request. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined return and alternate planning.
texts_above.4: SP had the return route, the alternate and the criteria for choosing between them ready before they could be needed, with the weather and the fuel needed for each refreshed at every operations check. Any change to the sortie was answered by the next best option already identified. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary return and alternate planning.

error_modes.label: DUTIES CARRIED OUT WITH MINIMUM IP SUPERVISION ACROSS THE SORTIE

texts.0: SP, due to waiting for direction on each step of the sortie, carried out none of the duties without the IP naming them. Departure checks, area management, radio work and the recovery were all started only on the IP's call, and no duty was begun on SP's own initiative. The IP had to take control to keep the sortie progressing, and the remaining profile was reduced.
texts.1: SP, due to a habit of confirming each duty with the IP before acting, needed continuous IP supervision through the departure, the area work and the recovery. The duties were carried out correctly once started, but each one began with a verbal prompt from the IP. The trend shows no reduction in that supervision across the sortie, which kept the performance at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to early reliance on the IP to open the phases of the sortie, needed prompts during the departure. SP then started the area duties and the recovery unaided and carried them out with minimum supervision. The prompts faded as the sortie developed and no IP input was required in the second half.
texts.3: SP carried out all duties with minimum IP supervision, starting each phase of the sortie from the briefed plan. The IP was used only as the safety observer.
texts.4: SP carried out every duty independently from engine start to engine shutdown and started each phase before it was due. The IP's supervision stayed limited to the safety observation role.
texts.marginal: SP carried out the duties within the standard and with little supervision, but the start of the area phase and of the recovery still waited for a glance from the IP. The trend was toward confirming before acting. SP is expected to start each phase from the plan without checking first.

texts_at.0: SP carried out the departure, area and recovery duties with the IP naming each phase and checking each step, the habit of starting a phase unaided being new at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to open at least one phase of the sortie unprompted on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP carried out the sortie duties at the limit of what the standard allows, one phase of the sortie started only after the IP prompted it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to open each phase from the briefed plan, so the IP's supervision can fall to the safety observation role.
texts_at.2: SP carried out the sortie duties with minimum IP supervision, correcting without prompting a start to the area phase that had waited for the IP's call. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to open each phase from the plan without waiting, so no phase waits for a call.
texts_at.3: SP carried out the duties of the departure, the area work and the recovery with minimum IP supervision, with one phase started a moment after it could have been. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to start that phase as promptly as the rest.

texts_above.1: SP carried out the departure, area and recovery duties, with one phase started only after a verbal call from the IP. The remaining phases were opened from the briefed plan. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP opened the area phase and the recovery unaided after needing prompts at the start of the sortie, so the IP supervision fell as the flight progressed. Opening the departure from the plan as well would remove the early prompts. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady growth of independence through the sortie.
texts_above.3: SP carried out every duty of the sortie from the briefed plan with minimum IP supervision, started each phase on its own cue and kept the IP's role to safety observation. Departure, area work and recovery all showed the same independence. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise self-direction of the sortie duties.
texts_above.4: SP ran the whole sortie from the briefed plan, started each phase before the IP could prompt it and handled changes within the flight on its own initiative. The IP's role stayed that of a safety observer from engine start to engine shutdown. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding self-direction of the sortie duties.

error_modes.label: FLIGHT DISCIPLINE FROM PREPARATION TO DEBRIEF - GOVERNING GUIDELINES FOLLOWED IN SPIRIT AND INTENT

texts.0: SP, due to mission preparation that did not include study of the rules and procedures or of the profile, showed up unprepared to fly. The briefing questions could not be answered, the mission requirements were not understood before engine start, and the sortie was flown without the briefed plan. The IP had to take control to bring the execution back inside the governing guidelines.
texts.1: SP, due to preparation that covered the profile but not the governing guidelines, arrived at the briefing able to state the route but not the rules around it. Several mission requirements became clear only when the IP repeated them in the air. The execution followed the brief at the limit of the acceptable standard and had to be reinforced from outside the plan.
texts.2: SP, due to a gap in preparation on one set of guidelines, initially executed one phase differently from the brief. SP identified the difference against the briefing notes without prompting, stated it and returned to the briefed execution. The rest of the sortie followed the brief and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP arrived prepared to fly, having studied the profile and the applicable rules and procedures, and executed the mission as briefed and in accordance with the governing guidelines from engine start to engine shutdown. The debrief addressed flight discipline.
texts.4: SP prepared to a standard that allowed the whole profile, its rules and its restrictions to be briefed from memory, and executed it exactly as briefed. Flight discipline was evaluated in the debrief by SP before the IP raised it.
texts.marginal: SP prepared, briefed and executed the mission to the governing guidelines, but the study of the rules was less thorough than the study of the profile and one guideline needed a second look at the briefing. The trend was toward preparing the profile first and the guidelines second. SP is expected to give the rules and procedures equal preparation time.

texts_at.0: SP followed the preparation, the briefing and the execution of the sortie with the IP restating the governing guidelines in flight, the habit of working from them unaided being new at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to restate the main guidelines for the sortie before the IP does at the next briefing.
texts_at.1: SP prepared, briefed and executed the sortie inside the code 1 band, several guidelines becoming clear only after the IP restated them in flight. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to study the rules and procedures to the same depth as the profile, as Techniques and Procedures Manual 1.5 describes, so none needs restating in the air.
texts_at.2: SP prepared, briefed and executed the sortie to the governing guidelines, correcting without prompting one phase first flown differently from the brief. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to close each preparation gap before the briefing, so no phase departs from the brief.
texts_at.3: SP arrived prepared, briefed on time and executed the mission as briefed from engine start to engine shutdown, with one debrief point recognized a moment after the IP raised it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to recognize every debrief point before it is raised.

texts_above.1: SP prepared, briefed and executed the sortie to the governing guidelines, with one guideline restated after a verbal call from the IP. The rest of the sortie followed the brief unprompted. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the difference from the brief against the briefing notes without prompting, stated it and returned to the briefed execution for the rest of the sortie. Closing that preparation gap before the briefing would remove even that departure. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid preparation for the briefed execution.
texts_above.3: SP arrived prepared to fly, was on time and ready to brief, answered every question at the briefing and executed the mission as briefed in accordance with the governing guidelines from engine start to engine shutdown. The debrief was used to evaluate flight discipline, as Techniques and Procedures Manual 1.5 intends. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed adherence to the spirit and intent of the guidelines.
texts_above.4: SP prepared so thoroughly that the profile, the guidelines and their reasons could be briefed from memory and discussed in depth, and then flew the mission exactly as briefed to engine shutdown. The debrief of flight discipline began with SP's own assessment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional preparation for and adherence to the guidelines.
